title: Risperidone and Alcohol: Risks, Dizziness, and Safe Choices
excerpt: Can you drink on risperidone (Risperdal)? How the two interact, why fainting and sedation are the main risks, what to know about injections and missed doses, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on risperidone (Risperdal)? How it interacts with alcohol, why dizziness and sedation are the main risks, and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the official advice is to avoid alcohol while you take risperidone (brand name Risperdal). The US patient information for Risperdal tells people not to drink while on it, and the prescribing information asks doctors to use caution when risperidone is combined with alcohol or other drugs that act on the brain. One drink isn't known to be poisonous with risperidone. The problem is that both slow the brain down, both can drop your blood pressure, and together they can leave you drowsier, dizzier, and less coordinated than you expect. Alcohol can also work against the very condition risperidone is treating. The real-world risks are fainting and falls, impaired driving, overheating, and a rougher course for your mental health.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink at all while you're starting risperidone or after a dose change, because that's when dizziness and sleepiness are strongest. Never skip a dose, or delay an injection, so that you can drink. If you and your prescriber agree that an occasional drink is acceptable once you're stable, stick to the amount they set, have it with food and water, stand up slowly, and never drive afterward. If drinking is a regular part of your week, tell your prescriber plainly. They can't adjust your treatment for something they don't know about.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your diagnosis, dose, and other medicines. **Talk to your prescriber before drinking on risperidone,** especially if you take it for bipolar disorder or schizophrenia, are on a long-acting injection, take other sedating medicines, are over 65, or have a history of fainting, seizures, diabetes, or heavy drinking. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** someone on risperidone who has been drinking can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, faints and doesn't come round quickly, has a seizure, vomits while barely conscious, or develops a high fever with stiff muscles and confusion. If someone talks about harming themselves, call or text **988** (US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline) or 911.

## What Risperidone Is and Why People Take It

Risperidone is a prescription medicine in the group called atypical, or second-generation, antipsychotics. It has been on the market since the 1990s and is one of the most widely prescribed medicines in its class. In the US it's approved for:

- **Schizophrenia**, in adults and teenagers
- **Bipolar I disorder**, to treat manic or mixed episodes, either on its own or added to lithium or valproate
- **Irritability linked to autism** in children and teenagers, including aggression, tantrums, and self-injury

Doctors also sometimes prescribe it off-label in low doses for other problems. If you're on a small dose and not sure why it was chosen, ask your prescriber, because the reason matters for how risky drinking is for you.

Risperidone comes in several forms:

- **Tablets**, including orally dissolving tablets (Risperdal M-Tab and generics), usually taken once or twice a day
- **Oral solution**, often used for children or people who have trouble swallowing
- **Long-acting injections**, such as Risperdal Consta (every two weeks into a muscle) and newer under-the-skin options such as Perseris and Uzedy, given every month or longer

Inside the body, risperidone is turned into an active form called 9-hydroxyrisperidone, which is itself sold as a separate drug, paliperidone (Invega). Almost everything in this guide applies to paliperidone too.

## How Risperidone and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Risperidone works mainly by blocking two kinds of chemical receptors in the brain: dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. Dampening those signals is what helps settle psychosis and mania. But risperidone doesn't stop there. It also blocks two other receptors, and those side effects are exactly where alcohol causes trouble.

### 1. Stacked sedation

Risperidone blocks histamine H1 receptors, the same target as old-fashioned drowsy antihistamines. That's a big part of why sleepiness is one of its most common side effects, especially early on and at higher doses.

Alcohol is a depressant. It boosts GABA, the brain's main "slow down" signal, and blunts glutamate, the main "speed up" signal. Put the two together and the slowing-down effects add up. You can feel far more drunk after two drinks than you would off the medicine, your reactions get slower, and your judgment slips without you noticing. Combining them with any other sedating medicine, such as sleeping pills, benzodiazepines, opioid painkillers, or night-time cold remedies, stacks the effect further.

### 2. Low blood pressure and fainting

Risperidone also blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. These help your blood vessels tighten when you stand up, so blood keeps reaching your brain. Blocking them causes **orthostatic hypotension**, a sudden drop in blood pressure when you stand that can make you lightheaded or faint. The prescribing information specifically warns about this, and it's most likely in the first days of treatment and after the dose goes up.

Alcohol widens blood vessels and, because it makes you pee more, can leave you dehydrated. Both push blood pressure down. So the classic risky moment is standing up quickly from the sofa or getting out of bed in the night after drinking on risperidone. That's how people end up fainting in the bathroom and hitting their head.

### 3. Thinking, coordination, and driving

The risperidone label warns that it can impair judgment, thinking, and motor skills, and tells people not to drive or operate machinery until they know how it affects them. Alcohol impairs exactly the same abilities. Even a blood alcohol level well under the legal limit can be enough to make driving unsafe when it's added to a medicine like this.

### 4. Body temperature and swallowing

Antipsychotics can interfere with the body's ability to regulate its own temperature. The risperidone label warns about this, particularly with heavy exercise, hot weather, or dehydration. A summer party with dancing, sun, and drinks hits all three. Antipsychotics have also been linked to swallowing problems, and heavy drinking adds a risk of vomiting while drowsy, which is a choking danger.

### 5. Alcohol working against the treatment

This is the effect people talk about least, and it may matter most over time. Alcohol disturbs sleep, worsens anxiety and low mood in the days after drinking, and can make some people impulsive. For someone being treated for bipolar disorder or schizophrenia, those are not small things. Heavy drinking is linked with more relapses, more hospital stays, and people forgetting or giving up their medicine. Our guide to [alcohol and dopamine](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-dopamine) explains why alcohol has such a strong pull on the same brain system risperidone is trying to calm.

### What alcohol doesn't do

Alcohol isn't known to change risperidone blood levels in a big way. Risperidone is broken down mainly by a liver enzyme called CYP2D6, which isn't the main enzyme alcohol uses. So the danger isn't usually that alcohol makes the drug build up. It's that the two drugs' effects pile on top of each other. That's a key difference from some other medicines, and it means even a "normal" dose of risperidone plus a moderate amount of alcohol can cause problems.

## What the Label and Research Actually Say

**The label.** The US prescribing information for Risperdal notes that, given risperidone's main effects on the brain, caution should be used when it's taken with other centrally acting drugs and alcohol. The patient information goes further and tells people to avoid alcohol. The label also lists the warnings that alcohol can worsen: sleepiness, orthostatic hypotension and fainting, impaired thinking and motor skills, trouble regulating body temperature, and a lowered seizure threshold.

**The research.** There isn't much controlled research on giving people risperidone and alcohol together, for obvious ethical reasons. What we know comes mainly from the pharmacology described above, from the labels, and from studies of people with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder who also drink. Those studies consistently find that substance use, including alcohol, is common in these conditions and is linked with worse outcomes, including more relapses and lower medication adherence. That's not proof that every drink is harmful, but it explains why prescribers take the question seriously.

## Can You Drink on Risperidone at All?

The official answer is to avoid alcohol. In real life, prescribers sometimes have a more nuanced conversation with a patient who has been stable for a long time and wants to know if a single drink at a wedding is acceptable. That's a decision for you and your prescriber, not for an article. Some honest points to bring to that conversation:

- **How stable you are.** If your mood or symptoms have shifted recently, alcohol is a bigger risk.
- **Your dose and form.** Higher doses usually mean more sedation and more blood pressure effects.
- **Your other medicines.** Mood stabilizers, antidepressants, sleep aids, and anxiety medicines all change the picture. See our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) for how common ones interact.
- **Your drinking pattern.** One drink with dinner twice a year is a very different question from several drinks every weekend.

If you do get the go-ahead for an occasional drink, the practical rules are simple: only the amount your prescriber agreed, with food, alongside water, sitting down, at home or with someone you trust, and no driving for the rest of the day.

## Risperdal and Alcohol: Is the Brand Any Different?

No. Risperdal is the original brand name, and generic risperidone contains the same active drug. The interaction with alcohol is the same whether your bottle says Risperdal, risperidone, or a pharmacy's own label. The same applies to the orally dissolving tablets and the liquid. If you take paliperidone (Invega), the active form of risperidone, the same cautions apply, since it shares the same receptor effects.

## Risperidone Injections (Consta, Perseris, Uzedy) and Alcohol

Long-acting injections release risperidone slowly over weeks. That has two consequences for drinking.

First, **the drug is always in your system.** There's no "wait a few hours after your dose" trick, because the level is meant to stay steady. Any time you drink, you're drinking on risperidone.

Second, **you can't skip a dose to make room for a night out.** Some people are tempted to delay an injection before a holiday or a celebration. Don't. Delaying doesn't clear the drug quickly, and a gap in treatment raises the risk of symptoms returning. If an upcoming event is worrying you, talk to your care team before the appointment rather than missing it.

## Should You Skip a Dose of Risperidone to Drink?

No, and this is one of the most important points in the whole guide. Risperidone and its active form stay in your body for a day or more after a tablet, and for weeks after an injection, so skipping one dose doesn't make drinking safe. What skipping does do is raise the chance of your symptoms coming back, and stopping antipsychotics suddenly can cause withdrawal-type effects such as nausea, sweating, and sleep problems.

If you've already been drinking and it's time for your dose, call your pharmacist or prescriber for advice. Many will tell you to take your usual dose as normal if you've had one or two drinks, but they can give you an answer that fits your dose and timing. Don't double up later to make up for a missed dose.

## Does Risperidone Help With Alcohol Cravings?

Probably not, based on the evidence so far. Because alcohol's rewarding effects involve dopamine and risperidone blocks dopamine receptors, researchers have wondered whether it might reduce drinking. A handful of small studies have looked at risperidone and other antipsychotics in people who drink heavily, some of them in people who also have schizophrenia. The results have been mixed, and there is no good evidence that risperidone reduces drinking or cravings. It isn't approved for that use.

Medicines that are approved for alcohol use disorder, such as naltrexone and acamprosate, exist and can be used alongside antipsychotics in many cases. If you're trying to cut back and finding it hard, that's worth raising with your prescriber, who can look at options that fit with your current treatment.

## Hangovers on Risperidone

People on risperidone often report that alcohol hits them harder and that the next day feels worse. That fits the mechanism. The medicine's sedation can linger into the morning, alcohol-disturbed sleep piles on top, and low blood pressure plus dehydration can make you feel dizzy and washed out.

If you've had a drink and feel rough the next day:

- **Get up slowly.** Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before standing.
- **Drink water and have something to eat.** A salty snack and fluids can help with lightheadedness.
- **Skip extra sedating remedies.** Night-time cold medicines and "PM" painkillers contain antihistamines that add to risperidone's drowsiness.
- **Don't drive** until you're clearly back to normal.
- **Check pain relievers with a pharmacist.** Most people can use a standard dose of an ordinary painkiller, but it's worth checking alongside your other medicines.

If the dizziness is severe, you faint, or you feel confused, get medical help rather than sleeping it off.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

Most people who have a drink on risperidone feel unusually sleepy or lightheaded and nothing more. But a few situations need urgent care.

**Call 911 or go to the emergency room if someone on risperidone who has been drinking:**

- Can't be woken, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- Is breathing slowly, irregularly, or with long pauses
- Faints and doesn't recover quickly, or hits their head when falling
- Has a seizure
- Vomits while very drowsy (roll them onto their side to keep the airway clear)
- Develops a high fever, very stiff muscles, sweating, and confusion. This can be a rare but serious reaction to antipsychotics called neuroleptic malignant syndrome
- Feels extremely hot, stops sweating, or becomes confused after drinking in the heat

Our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) covers what to look for and what to do while you wait for help. And if mood drops sharply after drinking, or someone talks about not wanting to be alive, call or text **988** in the US, or call 911.

**Book a routine appointment with your prescriber if you notice:** dizziness when standing that doesn't settle, new muscle stiffness or restlessness, weight gain or increased thirst, or that your drinking has crept up since starting treatment.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

The risk from combining risperidone and alcohol is higher if you:

- **Are just starting risperidone or have had a dose increase.** Dizziness and sleepiness are strongest early on.
- **Are over 65.** Older adults are more prone to falls and low blood pressure. Risperidone also carries a boxed warning about increased risk of death in older people with dementia-related psychosis, a group in which it isn't approved.
- **Take other sedating medicines**, such as benzodiazepines, sleeping pills, opioids, or sedating antidepressants.
- **Take blood pressure medicines**, which can add to the drop in pressure.
- **Have diabetes or high blood sugar.** Risperidone can affect blood sugar, weight, and cholesterol, and alcohol can push blood sugar up or down unpredictably.
- **Have a history of seizures.** Antipsychotics can lower the seizure threshold, and heavy drinking and alcohol withdrawal both raise seizure risk.
- **Are a teenager.** Risperidone is approved for some under-18s, and alcohol is riskier for the developing brain. Parents and young people should talk this through with the prescriber.

## How Risperidone Compares With Other Antipsychotics

Every antipsychotic carries a "be careful with alcohol" message, but the details differ. Medicines that are more sedating, such as quetiapine and olanzapine, tend to produce stronger drowsiness when combined with alcohol. Risperidone sits in the middle for sedation but stands out for its effect on blood pressure when you stand up. Aripiprazole is usually less sedating, though the same basic advice applies. If you want to compare, see our guides to [Seroquel and alcohol](/never-hungover/seroquel-and-alcohol), [olanzapine and alcohol](/never-hungover/olanzapine-and-alcohol), [Abilify and alcohol](/never-hungover/abilify-and-alcohol), and [Latuda and alcohol](/never-hungover/latuda-and-alcohol). If you also take a mood stabilizer, our [lithium and alcohol](/never-hungover/lithium-and-alcohol) guide is worth a read.

## What About DHM and Other Hangover Supplements?

You may come across DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound sold as a hangover supplement. It's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver, mostly in animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that it reduces the sedation, low blood pressure, or other combined effects of risperidone and alcohol. It hasn't been studied in people taking antipsychotics, and it doesn't make drinking on risperidone safe.

If you're on risperidone, no supplement makes alcohol safer with it, so check with your prescriber or pharmacist before adding anything, DHM included. We don't recommend hangover products on this page. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about DHM alongside common medicines, and our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) summarizes how the main drug classes interact with alcohol. For hangovers in general, the habits in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) matter far more than any pill.

## The Bottom Line

- The official advice is to avoid alcohol on risperidone.
- The main risks are stacked sedation, sudden drops in blood pressure that cause fainting and falls, impaired driving, overheating, and alcohol undermining your treatment.
- Alcohol doesn't change risperidone levels much. The danger comes from the two drugs' effects adding together.
- Never skip a tablet or delay an injection so you can drink.
- If your prescriber agrees an occasional drink is acceptable, stick to the amount they set, with food and water, stand up slowly, and don't drive.
- Get emergency help for unresponsiveness, slow breathing, seizures, fainting with injury, or high fever with stiff muscles.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking risperidone?**

The official advice is to avoid it. The patient information for Risperdal tells people not to drink, and the prescribing information calls for caution when combining risperidone with alcohol. Both slow the brain down and both can lower blood pressure, so together they can cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness, fainting, and impaired driving. If you've been stable for a long time and want to have an occasional drink, discuss it with your prescriber first.

**What happens if you drink on Risperdal?**

Most often, people feel much drowsier, more lightheaded, and less coordinated than they would from the same amount of alcohol alone. Standing up quickly can cause a sudden drop in blood pressure and fainting. Larger amounts raise the risk of falls, vomiting while drowsy, breathing problems, and dangerous decisions. Over time, regular drinking can also make the condition risperidone treats harder to control.

**How long after taking risperidone can I drink?**

There's no safe waiting window. Risperidone and its active form stay in the body for a day or more after a tablet, and they're meant to stay at a steady level when you take them every day. With a long-acting injection, the drug is in your system continuously. Any time you drink, you're drinking on risperidone, so the question to ask your prescriber is whether any alcohol is acceptable for you, not how long to wait.

**Should I skip my risperidone dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Skipping a dose doesn't clear the drug quickly enough to make drinking safe, and missing doses raises the risk of symptoms coming back. Stopping suddenly can also cause withdrawal-type effects. If you've already had a drink and your dose is due, call your pharmacist or prescriber for advice, and don't double up later.

**Is it safe to drink on a risperidone injection like Risperdal Consta or Perseris?**

The same cautions apply as with tablets, and there's no way to time drinks around the dose because the injection releases medicine steadily for weeks. Don't delay or skip an injection to make room for drinking. If an upcoming event is worrying you, talk to your care team before your appointment.

**Does risperidone reduce alcohol cravings?**

There is no good evidence that it does. A few small studies have looked at antipsychotics, including risperidone, in people who drink heavily, and the results have been mixed. Risperidone isn't approved for treating alcohol use. If you want to cut back, ask your prescriber about medicines that are approved for that purpose and work alongside your current treatment.

**Can I take DHM while on risperidone?**

DHM hasn't been studied in people taking antipsychotics, and there is no good evidence that it reduces the combined effects of risperidone and alcohol. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist before adding any supplement to risperidone. Even if they say it's fine, it doesn't change the advice to avoid or strictly limit alcohol.
